howToMeasure: Put cuff on upper arm, heart level
bp_systolic.whyItMatters: Blood pressure can drop after weeks in weightlessness. Low pressure raises the risk of fainting when gravity returns.

bp_diastolic.whyItMatters: It shows how your blood vessels are adapting to weightlessness. A change from your own usual number is what matters.

howToMeasure: Put the sensor on your finger
heart_rate.whyItMatters: Your heart adapts to weightlessness and can struggle when gravity returns. A change from your usual number is an early sign.

howToMeasure: Touch the drop to the strip
glucose.whyItMatters: Glucose shows how your body handles food and rest in a closed cabin. A change from your usual matters more than one number.

howToMeasure: Wait after exercise or hot drinks
body_temp.whyItMatters: Your defenses change in space, and germs pass easily between people in a closed cabin. A small rise can be an early sign.

sleep_hours.whyItMatters: Short or broken sleep makes isolation harder and lowers focus. Light therapy can help reset your body clock.

howToMeasure: Pick the level that fits right now
mood.whyItMatters: Isolation, short sleep and heavy workload can lower mood and focus. Noticing it early lets you act before it affects the mission.

headache_score.whyItMatters: Headache can come from cabin CO₂, low oxygen or poor sleep. Reporting it helps us find the cause.

symptom_dizziness.whyItMatters: Dizziness is common while your balance system adapts to new gravity. It can also come from low blood pressure.

symptom_vision.whyItMatters: Fluids shifting toward the head can press on the eyes. About 70 % of ISS astronauts show some eye swelling.

howToMeasure: Answer yes if either felt hard
symptom_confusion.whyItMatters: Confusion is one of the signs of low oxygen. It is easy to miss in yourself, so report it early.

howToMeasure: Note any joint ache or pain
Think about the last pressure change
symptom_joint_pain.whyItMatters: Joint pain after a pressure change can be a sign of decompression sickness. Stop the activity and report it.

howToMeasure: Look at your skin and lips
Note any rash or cold sore
Note any new itch or allergy
symptom_skin.whyItMatters: Dormant viruses can wake up in space, and the immune system changes. Cold sores and rashes are early signs.

howToMeasure: Clip the sensor on a finger
spo2.whyItMatters: SpO₂ shows how much oxygen your blood carries. Low-oxygen risk is small, but worth watching in a sealed cabin.

cabin_co2.whyItMatters: NASA limits cabin CO₂ to 3 mmHg as a 1-hour average. Headaches have been reported from about 2.8 mmHg.

exercise_min.whyItMatters: NASA's target is 1.5 hours a day, 6–7 days a week. Exercise is the main way to slow bone and muscle loss.

howToMeasure: Add up the water you drank
water_ml.whyItMatters: Dehydration plus calcium released from bone raises kidney stone risk. Fluids also help prevent fainting at landing.

howToMeasure: Enter your result as a percent
strength_self_pct.whyItMatters: Fitness drops 10–12 % on average in space; 12–38 % of crew lose more than 20 %. Weekly checks catch the slide early.
